Your end-to-end tests break every time someone renames a button - the test was just glued to a CSS class. 
So I built CI that tests your app in plain English and heals itself when the UI changes. Runs on every PR. npx agentic-e2e init https://t.co/URpAN2FeQn

Most teams don’t struggle with writing tests. They struggle with keeping them alive. 

In fact, nearly 45% of automation budgets get eaten up by pure maintenance. 

Every time the UI changes, tests break. Flaky tests pile up. Releases slow down. 

Teams usually blame the tool. They switch from Selenium to Cypress, or Cypress to Playwright. 

But tools only run scripts. Your framework decides how much maintenance you get stuck with. 

Every framework solves one problem and creates another: 
- Linear is fast to build, impossible to scale.
- Data-driven expands coverage, explodes data management.
- Keyword-driven helps non-coders, demands heavy upkeep.
- Hybrid gives flexibility, requires strict governance. 

If your automation feels like technical debt, it is time to rethink the foundation.

👉Swipe through the slides to see how the most common frameworks stack up.

Read the full breakdown here:
https://hubs.li/Q04w26k20

#TestAutomation #QualityEngineering #SoftwareTesting #DevOps #QAAutomation

🚀 nx9-wg is not another WireGuard panel.

There are already plenty of tools that create peers, generate QR codes and bring up WireGuard.

The harder problem is:

What happens after the configuration is applied?

Most WG management stacks look roughly like:

🌐 Web UI
↓
📄 Config files
↓
⚙️ wg / wg-quick
↓
🔧 ip / nft / sysctl
↓
🐧 Linux kernel
That works.

But a VPN control plane for a router, CPE, SD-WAN appliance or private WAN needs something more.
🧠 nx9-wg is built around desired state and reconciliation.
SQLite stores authoritative desired state.
The reconciliation engine compares it with live system state.

Then nx9-wg talks directly to Linux through:
🔹 WireGuard Generic Netlink
🔹 RTNETLINK for links, addresses and routes
🔹 libnftables. so.1 for firewall and NAT
🔹 procfs for forwarding

❌ No wg subprocess.
❌ No wg-quick.
❌ No ip subprocess.
❌ No nft subprocess.
❌ No Node runtime.
❌ No Python runtime in the appliance path.

Just one Rust binary coordinating the network state.

That architectural difference matters.
🔄 Why does reconciliation matter for a VPN?
A VPN is not:
create peer → generate QR → done

It is a live relationship between:
👤 peers
📡 interfaces
📍 tunnel addresses
🛣️ routes
🔥 firewall policy
🌐 NAT
↔️ forwarding
💾 persistent state
🐧 kernel state

And systems drift.

Someone changes a route manually.

A peer disappears from the database but remains active in the kernel.

A firewall rule changes.

A reboot reconstructs only part of the expected state.

Docker, CNI, libvirt or another networking component changes something underneath you.

The dangerous failure is often silent divergence.

The database says one thing.

The kernel is doing another.

nx9-wg treats:
💾 SQLite = authoritative desired state
🐧 Linux kernel = live state
🔄 reconciliation = convergence mechanism

The lifecycle is:
Plan → Apply → Verify → Converged
Or:
PartialFailure / DriftRemains
If the system is already converged, applying the same desired state should be a no-op.
That is a much more useful property than another dashboard.

📡 Why does this matter for CPE firmware?
➡️ Routers and CPE devices have different constraints from a desktop Linux server.

You want:
⚡ small runtime footprint
🔒 explicit privilege boundaries
💾 deterministic persistent state
🔄 predictable reboot recovery
🧩 simple integration
🐧 native Linux networking
🛠️ diagnosability without a cloud dependency

A CPE should be able to reboot at 03:00, read its persistent state, reconstruct the required kernel state, reconcile it, verify it and become converged again.

That is a firmware problem.

Not a UI problem.

The same model can apply to:
🏠 SMB routers
📡 broadband CPE
🌐 SD-WAN appliances
🏭 industrial gateways
🏢 managed VPN appliances
🛰️ private WAN edge devices
📶 small ISP infrastructure

The useful abstraction becomes:
interface → peer → address allocation → route → firewall → NAT → forwarding → diagnostics → backup

A vendor can build its own product experience around that control plane instead of rebuilding the networking state machine from scratch.

📜 And the license matters.

nx9-wg is MIT OR Apache-2.0.
That is intentional.

A firmware vendor can potentially:
🔧 integrate the binary
📦 vendor the crates
🧩 add board-specific integration
🔍 audit the Netlink implementation
🏗️ build its own product layer
🚀 ship it as part of a commercial appliance

without introducing a copyleft requirement.

✅ Apache-2.0 provides an explicit patent grant.
✅ MIT keeps the licensing model simple.

❌ No license server.
❌ No mandatory cloud.
❌ No telemetry requirement.
❌ No SaaS dependency.

For vendors building networking products, that flexibility matters.

🏢 What about small and medium-sized companies?

They do not necessarily need another VPN SaaS dashboard.

They need infrastructure they can own.
nx9-wg is aimed at capabilities such as:
🔐 site-to-site VPN
👨‍💻 road-warrior access
🏠 private LAN access
👥 peer lifecycle management
💾 backup and restore
📋 auditability
🔎 diagnostics
🖥️ CLI + Web UI
💾 persistent desired state
without making the company's network dependent on somebody else's subscription.

The expensive failure is not:
"Our dashboard needs another widget."

It is:
"The tunnel is up, the route is wrong, and nobody knows why."

Reconciliation gives you somewhere to start answering that question.

⚠️ One important WireGuard invariant

Server-side AllowedIPs and client-side full-tunnel policy are not the same thing.

For server peers, nx9-wg derives /32 or /128 cryptokey routes from assigned tunnel addresses.
A client wanting:
0.0.0.0/0
for full-tunnel traffic is a different concern.
Conflating those two concepts is an easy way to break a multi-peer VPN.
That distinction belongs in the control plane.

Not in a UI dropdown.

🧪 And I'm not going to oversell the validation.

Physical validation has been performed.

The multi-path remote LAN scenario was tested across:
📱 cellular 5G
📶 Wi-Fi
📱 phone STA + AP hop
💻 SSH access into the protected LAN

But throughput soak and roaming-during-session are not being claimed as completed validation.

Unit tests matter.

They are not a substitute for a real client on the other side of a real tunnel.

That distinction matters in networking software.
🧠 The idea behind nx9-wg is simple:
💾 Desired state lives in SQLite.
🐧 Live state lives in the Linux kernel.
🔄 Reconciliation sits between them.
🔐 The operator keeps control of the infrastructure.

That is what makes nx9-wg interesting to me.

Not another pretty WireGuard panel.

A native Linux control plane that can potentially sit underneath:
📡 a CPE
🌐 a router
🏭 an industrial gateway
🏢 an SMB network
🛰️ a private WAN
🚀 or a commercial networking product

Most of you know I'm a fan of stacked diffs. They got popularized because of Gerrit, Phabricator and more VCS that worked with changes (commits) as the unit of review. A few years ago, @GergelyOrosz wrote a great article about it too.

At Adevinta, some people built maiao to brigde the gap between GitHub and the way some parts of the company worked, with Gerrit. 

After a Private Equity fund took over, the maintainers left the company and we brought it back as a fork, under a new GH org umbrella.

Maiao v1.4 is out and it got featured on Hacker News yesterday! It gives you `git review`. Each commit in your branch becomes its own stacked PR/MR, with automatic parent-child dependencies.

What's new since the last time I shared it? Now it supports GitHub, @cursor Origin, GitLab, Gitea, Forgejo (e.g., Codeberg), and Bitbucket Cloud.

The Lobsters/Hackernews discussion brought up a good point: there are many tools in this space: Graphite (now part of SpaceX/Cursor), jj, and others.

What makes maiao different? It's "just git." No new model, no new API, no CLI to learn beyond `git review`. Everything is a git commit. The automation is transparent.

Tools like Graphite introduce "stack" as a first-class concept with its own UI and commands. That might give a better experience, but at the cost of diverging from plain git. And Graphite monetized it.

Maiao has none of these goals. It's a single Go binary. MIT licensed. No account needed.

Someone in the thread said stacked commits are fundamentally at odds with GitHub's design and that we need a new kind of forge. I tend to agree, but:

a) GitHub is the default. It's not practical to ask the critical mass to switch.
b) In many companies, you don't get to choose your forge.

So the pragmatic approach: a progressive enhancement that doesn't break anyone else's flow. Your teammates keep reviewing PRs as usual. You get to work with granular, single-purpose commits.

No one else needs to change anything. Small, contained commits also make reviews dramatically better. A 50-line PR with one logical change is reviewable in minutes. A 500-line PR with three concerns mixed together? That sits in the queue for days.

Stacked diffs let you ship the same total work, but in pieces a human can actually reason about. And here's something that matters more every day: in a world where AI agents produce a lot of code, CI becomes the critical gate before trunk.

A stacked PR isn't just a review unit. It's a CI unit. Each PR runs its own pipeline. Failures are isolated to one logical change, not buried in a mega-diff. When an agent generates a feature across multiple concerns (schema change, business logic, API endpoint, tests), you get:

a) CI runs in parallel across the stack
b) A failure in one layer doesn't block feedback on the others
c) You can merge the bottom of the stack while fixing the top

en your existing OpenAI API client can talk to the local model with no code changes, since LM Studio mimics the OpenAI protocol
                     * http://inero-software.com
                     * . Recommendation: implement a configuration where the base URL and API key for each provider can be overridden. For example, a toggle “Use local model” could switch the OpenAI base URL to local and use a dummy key. Ensure your model service is flexible: it should allow different endpoints and not assume cloud. Another tool to watch is LocalAI (a drop-in local OpenAI API emulator using llama.cpp) – similar concept to LM Studio’s server. By structuring your code to call a base URL, switching to any of these is trivial. Finally, consider packaging a basic local model with the app for offline mode – e.g., a 3B param model for simple tasks – but only if it can run efficiently on most hardware. This might be done in an Electron context or via a companion binary. In any case, architect for pluggable model backends: local or remote. This will maximize flexibility as the landscape of local LLMs evolves.
                     * Secure API Key Management: Security of API keys and any credentials is paramount, especially as you integrate many providers. In development, .env files and environment variables are fine (and you correctly avoided exposing keys in the React app by using a service layer
                     * Google Drive
                     * ). For production, take it further: use a secret management system. If deploying on Vercel, use their encrypted secret storage for environment vars; on AWS, you might use AWS Secrets Manager or Parameter Store to inject keys into your container’s env at runtime. Ensure that no keys are ever sent to the client. The client app should not even know which provider is being called except in abstract terms. For instance, if the user selects “GPT-5”, the front-end just sends that as a parameter to your backend – the backend then picks the corresponding API key and endpoint. This prevents any possibility of leaking the keys via browser dev tools. Additionally, implement role-based access if needed: e.g., maybe only your account can use the Gemini key if it’s high-cost, while other users default to open models – depending on your usage plans. On the desktop side, continue the pattern of not hardcoding keys into the app bundle. OmniMind’s Electron mode stored keys in electron/.env and passed requests via IPC
                     * Google Drive
                     *  – that’s a solid approach. You could enhance it by encrypting the key at rest (even a simple XOR or encryption with a hardcoded phrase is better than plain text, though storing in OS keychain would be ideal). Also consider the case of keys for local models (not sensitive, but the path or model name might be user-specific) – those can be in a config file but treat them carefully if they point to local resources. If your platform will allow user-provided API keys (say a user wants to plug in their own OpenAI key), you’ll need to store those per user securely – possibly in a database with encryption. In web, you’d then need user accounts and a secure backend storage. In short, use backend-only storage for all secrets and minimize their footprint in memory, and ensure your code never logs them. Following these practices will protect your valuable high-tier credentials from misuse
                     * Google Drive
                     * .
                     * Auto-Scaling & External Compute Services: To handle unpredictable loads or heavy tasks, take advantage of specialized AI hosting services:
                     * RunPod: Great for running custom models or jobs in the cloud. You can deploy a container with your model or use their serverless autoscaling. It’s very flexible (supports arbitrary CUDA code) and is cost-effective. Notably, RunPod’s serverless offering has very fast cold starts (~seconds to spin up a GPU container) and can scale globally
                     * http://ankursnewsletter.com
                     * . This is an excellent option if, for example, you allow users to execute some code or you host a particular open-source model yourself. You’d integrate by calling their API to start jobs or using their HTTP endpoint for deployed pods. They also have a CLI and API that could be automated from your backend when load increases.
                     * http://Together.ai: Ideal if you want a managed solution for open models. Together offers an inference API that includes many popular models and even optimizations that make them faster than stock (they claim up to 75% faster than standard PyTorch for LLMs)
                     * http://ankursnewsletter.com
                     * . They also provide an OpenAI-compatible API layer
                     * http://ankursnewsletter.com
                     * . Using Together, you could hit an endpoint like http://api.together.ai/gpt-j with your request and get a response, without hosting anything yourself. Pricing is often per-token. This could augment your platform by providing a fallback if OpenAI/Gemini quotas are hit, or to offer models that you don’t have keys for (e.g. open alternatives like Falcon, etc.). Integration is straightforward via HTTP calls with an API key.
                     * Others: You mentioned http://Banana.dev; as noted, Banana’s original service shut down
                     * http://banana.dev
                     * , but the concept lives on in alternatives. If considering Modal or Anyscale – those are more developer-centric but powerful (Modal gives a serverless Python API approach, and Anyscale (Ray) is more for custom distributed workloads). These might be overkill initially, but could be useful if you build something like an AI that trains or fine-tunes models on the fly. Replicate is another option for quick model hosting; they have a library of community-provided model endpoints and also allow custom ones. For auto-scaling, the simplest path is to use providers like RunPod that abstract Kubernetes scaling for you. In practice, you might deploy a pool of model workers that auto-scale: e.g., 0 running normally, and when a request comes, it boots one. Using their APIs, you can programmatically scale up/down based on your current load (or even let their platform handle it via request triggers).
                     * Recommendation: Draft an architecture for how your backend will decide between local, self-hosted, and third-party API models. For example: if user selects a model that we label as “external API”, just call that API; if they select one labeled “self-hosted”, route to our RunPod deployment; if “local”, route to localhost. This routing logic can be part of the ModelService. By Phase 3, test out one of these services (say deploy a small model on RunPod serverless and integrate it as a new model option in OmniMind). This will give you experience with the ecosystem and ensure your app is ready to scale via these platforms when needed.
                     * Front-End Stack (Angular + Tailwind): On the client side, Angular is a solid choice for a large app with many features, providing structure (modules, services, etc.) out of the box. Use Angular’s built-in tooling (Angular CLI) to set up your project with Tailwind. Tailwind can be integrated by adding it to the angular.json build config or using a custom webpack if needed. The benefits of Tailwind are rapid UI development and consistency – define a design system early (colors, spacing, etc.) using Tailwind classes so that your components look cohesive. Since the previous UI used “Tailwind-like” classes
                     * Google Drive
                     * , you likely already have a style guide to follow. Leverage Angular’s service providers pattern to mirror what you had in React: for example, create an AiService in Angular that calls your backend (similar to the earlier geminiService in concept). This Angular service can manage state as needed or simply perform HTTP calls and return Observables/Promises to components. Use Angular’s module separation to isolate features (e.g., have a ChatModule, CodeModule, etc., each with its components and maybe sub-routes if needed for different sub-features). This will keep the app maintainable as it grows. For state management, Angular’s built-in services with RxJS may suffice, but if the app grows complex, consider NgRx or another state library in Phase 3 for more predictable state handling (the React version avoided external state libraries
                     * Google Drive
                     * , but at scale a unidirectional state management might help). Additionally, ensure web-worker or off-main-thread processing for heavy tasks if any on front-end (for example, if you do some client-side text embedding or local model inference for small models, do it in a web worker to keep the UI responsive). Lastly, optimize bundling – use Angular’s production build which does tree shaking; consider lazy-loading modules (e.g., don’t load the video generation component until the user navigates there). This will keep initial load fast, which is important for user experience.
In summary, use a scalable, high-performance backend (leaning Node for ease or Bun for speed), design for both cloud and local model usage, safeguard all credentials, utilize specialized AI infra to handle scale, and build a robust Angular front-end with modular architecture and Tailwind UI. This combination will give you a flexible and powerful stack that can evolve as your platform grows.
Modularizing AI Agent Actions Across Features
To make OmniMind Pro’s AI behavior flexible and extensible, it’s wise to modularize the “agent” actions – essentially breaking down what the AI can do into reusable, composable units. The key actions mentioned are build, reply, iterate, which map well to a variety of scenarios (coding, chatting, visual generation) with slightly different meanings. Here’s how to modularize them:
                     * Define Core Agent Actions: Create an abstraction for an AI “agent action.” For example, define an interface or base class AgentAction with a method like execute(context): ActionResult. Then implement specific actions like BuildAction, ReplyAction, IterateAction. Build might mean “produce an initial output from scratch given a request” (e.g. generate a new code snippet or create a new image). Reply typically means “provide an answer or continuation given the current state” (e.g. answer the user’s question in chat, or provide the next chunk of code in an ongoing coding session). Iterate means “take an existing output and refine/improve it” (e.g. take the code from build, run tests or analyze it, then fix bugs; or take an image and apply modifications). By formalizing these actions, you can then mix-and-match them in different sequences depending on the feature. For instance, a code assistant agent could be composed of [BuildAction, IterateAction] in a loop, whereas a Q&A chat agent might primarily use [ReplyAction] unless a tool is invoked. Each action implementation will use one or more models under the hood, but the higher-level agent logic doesn’t need to know specifics – it just calls execute() on the next action with the right context. This separation also means if you create a new type of action (say, a “ValidateAction” that checks something), you can slot it in without changing the others.
                     * Apply to Coding Pipeline: In the coding IDE module, design the AI workflow as a pipeline of these actions. For example: when the user requests code, the Code Agent will (1) perform a BuildAction to generate an initial solution (this might call GPT-4 or Gemini with a prompt “Write code to do X” using context of the file/project), (2) perform an IterateAction to self-review or test the code (this could involve running the code if possible, or using a static analysis model or even the same model with a prompt “Review the code for errors and improve it”), and potentially loop the iterate step a few times or until quality is acceptable, then (3) use a ReplyAction to present the final code to the user with an explanation. This resembles a sequential orchestration pattern where each stage’s output is improved by the next. You can implement this as a series of function calls or as an actual queue of AgentActions that the agent goes through. By modularizing, you could also let the user intervene: e.g. user could say “iterate again” to trigger another iteration, or skip it. Moreover, the same actions can be repurposed: a ReplyAction in coding might be used to answer conceptual questions (like “explain this code”). The BuildAction in coding could be used for creating new files or scaffolding projects (tying into the Rocket.new-like feature).pply to Chat Pipeline: In a general chat (non-coding context), the most common action is Reply. The chat agent mostly needs to generate a helpful response. However, modularizing still helps if you introduce tools. For example, you might have a BuildAction representing “use a tool to gather information” (like perform a search or calculation) and then a ReplyAction to produce the answer. An IterateAction could be used in a conversational sense if the assistant wants to refine a draft (though that’s less common in straightforward QA). Nonetheless, by having the same interface, your chat agent can also orchestrate multiple steps when needed. Think of a scenario: User asks a complex question, the agent decides to break it down – this could be modeled as the agent dynamically inserting a BuildAction (“find relevant info”) before the ReplyAction (“answer the user”). If using frameworks like LangChain or OpenAI function calling, you essentially are doing this: defining actions/tools and letting the model choose them. Your modular actions can integrate with that – e.g., you expose BuildAction as a function the model can call. Designing it yourself gives you more control and transparency.
                     * Apply to Visual Pipeline: For image/video generation, the loop might be: BuildAction = generate the initial asset from prompt, IterateAction = apply an edit or generate a variation. For example, the user generates an image, and then says “make it brighter” – that could trigger an IterateAction with a stable diffusion editor model. A ReplyAction here might simply acknowledge or describe the changes (“Here is the edited image”). By keeping these actions abstract, your image module could reuse the same IterateAction class as the code module but configured with different implementation (e.g., in code it runs tests, in images it calls an editing model). In practice you might implement them separately if too different, but at least conceptually you separate “initial creation” from “refinement”, which maps well to how artists work (draft vs revision) and how code is written (first version vs debug).
                     * Agent Controller & State: To manage these actions, create an Agent Controller that holds the state of the agent (current context, intermediate results, etc.) and a list of available actions. For each feature (chat, code, image), you might subclass or configure the controller with which actions to use. For example, CodeAgentController knows to use [Build, Iterate, Reply] in sequence for a given request. The controller feeds each action the necessary context: for Build it might be the user’s prompt and current file context; for Iterate, it might include the code output from Build plus any runtime results; for Reply, it has the final content to present. This controller can also log the process, which is great for debugging (and even for explaining to the user how the AI arrived at an answer, if you want to display that). By modularizing this way, you also open up the possibility for parallel or conditional flows later – e.g., you could try two BuildActions with different models in parallel and pick the best result, or have an IterateAction only run if the user requests refinement. The architecture from Microsoft’s guidance suggests that specialization and multi-agent orchestration improve scalability and maintainability
                     * http://learn.microsoft.com
                     *  – you’re doing exactly that by splitting the agent’s duties into focused units.
                     * Reusability and Testing: With actions as independent units, you can unit test them in isolation. For instance, test the BuildAction with a known prompt and a stubbed model response to see if it produces the expected intermediate format. This is much harder to do with one giant “monolithic” AI function. Reusability comes into play if you add more features: imagine later you add a documentation assistant that can generate docs from code – it might reuse the BuildAction (to generate documentation text) and IterateAction (to improve formatting) from the chat domain, for example. Consistent interfaces also mean you could enable user-defined workflows in the future (“chain these actions in a custom way”), giving advanced users a way to script the AI – a potential unique feature.
In summary, think of “build, reply, iterate” as fundamental verbs in an AI workflow. Implement each as a module that can work across different contexts. Then assemble them like Lego blocks for each specific feature’s needs. This will result in cleaner code, easier debugging, and a more powerful system design where improvements to one action (say you make IterateAction smarter for code) can benefit other areas if applicable. Competitors may have similar hidden architectures, but by making it explicit and modular, you’ll be able to innovate faster and ensure each part of the “AI brain” is specialized and excellent at its task
http://learn.microsoft.com
. It’s a design that mirrors human problem-solving (draft -> review -> refine) and will make your AI’s operations more transparent and controllable.
